chunks: My father narrated to us, may God be pleased with him, saying: Ali ibn Ibrahim narrated from his father, from Al-Nawfaly, from Al-Sakoony, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father (peace be upon them both).

He said: Abu Dharr (may God have Mercy upon him) stood by the Ka'ba and said, 'I am Jundab ibn Sakan.' The people gathered around him. He said, 'If one of you intended to travel, he would take provisions to sustain him. The journey of the Day of Resurrection is coming; do you not want to take what will sustain you?' A man stood up to him and said, 'Guide us.' He said, 'Fast on a day of intense heat for the Resurrection, and perform a Hajj for the major affairs. Pray two units in the darkness of the night for the loneliness of the graves. Speak a word of good and remain silent from a word of evil, or give charity from you to a poor person, perhaps you may be saved by it, O one who submits, from the Day of Hardship. Consider this world to be two Dirhams: one Dirham you spend on your family, and one Dirham you send ahead for your Hereafter. The third is harmful and does not benefit, so do not return it (keep it). Consider this world to be two words: one word in seeking the Halal (permissible sustenance) and one word for the Hereafter. The third is harmful and does not benefit, so do not return it.' Then he said, 'A sorrow killed me on a day I could not attain.'
ai.seo_question: How should a Muslim balance worldly life and the afterlife according to Abu Dharr?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Khisal*, Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) transmits Abu Dharr al-Ghifari’s eschatological advice, emphasizing that the journey to the Hereafter requires spiritual provisions akin to physical travel supplies. The metaphor of the world as 'two dirhams' and 'two words' underscores the Shia scholarly principle of moderation, where one dirham supports the family and the other secures the afterlife, while the third is superfluous. This teaching highlights the practical application of *zuhd* (asceticism) not as total renunciation, but as a balanced allocation of resources for both worldly duties and eternal salvation.
